name: PCB Fabrication

claims.claim_text: A two-layer board passes through roughly fifteen distinct manufacturing steps, and a multi-layer board through substantially more.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's like 15 different step, manufacturing steps, which goes into making a two-layer board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Project Management, Lasers & Robots - Staunch Specialty Sanctanimity

claims.claim_text: A full bare-board fabrication line runs to twenty-five or thirty steps, with cleanroom stages that must be re-entered in sequence.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was 25 or 30 steps
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: Drilling comes at the start of the process, before plating: the holes for vias and through-hole parts are drilled into the raw copper-clad board so the barrels can then be plated. A mid-sized fab runs rooms of multi-spindle CNC drills operating in parallel.
claims.quote_verbatim: you take the raw copper board and you drill holes where all the holes need to be drilled so that you can plate the through holes
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: Minimum via size is set by the drill: below the smallest mechanical drill bit the hole must be laser-drilled, which is an additional process step that many fabs do not have on site, so the job is subcontracted or refused.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you make them too small, they like can't use a drill bit anymore and they have to use a laser
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: Traces are output as a positive image and copper planes as a negative one, so on the plane layers of a Gerber set the areas that appear blank are where copper remains. Reading a plane layer as if it were positive inverts its meaning.
claims.quote_verbatim: planes are produced as a negative photo mask. So it appears inverse
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The negative convention is a legacy of manual layout: only negative photoresist board stock was available, so a positive taped artwork had to be converted to a negative on film before exposure, making board production a two-step photographic process.
claims.quote_verbatim: You had negative photo resist PCBs. They're really the only ones you could get at the time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: One way to eliminate the negative-conversion step was to lay the artwork out mirrored in the first place, trading a physical processing stage for a design-side inversion.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can skip a physical construction step. And if I actually lay everything out backwards
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: United States and Asian fabs differ in process, not only in price: environmental rules on etchant disposal shape the chemistry available, so in a US fab any hole with a copper pad on both sides is plated and anything else is not, while Asian fabs use a different resist that allows a single pass where the US process needs multiple steps.
claims.quote_verbatim: in a U.S. fab, the difference between a plated via and an unplated one is if there's a copper on both sides
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Drill density is a real panel-level constraint: above roughly forty holes per square inch averaged over the panel, fabs object, because drilling time and bit wear dominate that part of the process.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fab gets cranky if I give them a panel with more than about 40 holes per square inch
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Uneven copper coverage across a panel causes plating to run unevenly, producing breaks and shorts that the fab must hand-correct. A shared panel assembled from unrelated designs is especially prone to it, and fabs will refuse panels that force hundreds of manual fixes.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you don't have, um, consistent copper coverage across your panel, then you're going to have plating issues
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: An any-layer stack-up, where a laser via can connect any adjacent pair of layers, requires a lamination, plating and drilling cycle between each layer as the board is built up; an eight-layer any-layer board needs about five plating cycles, and that sequence, not the layer count alone, is what makes the board expensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: now you have to now you have a lamination plating and drilling cycle between each layer
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: Laser vias in an any-layer build can be stacked directly on top of each other or staggered; stacking is harder on yield and some manufacturers will not accept it, so the choice belongs to the fab's capability rather than the designer's preference.
claims.quote_verbatim: some manufacturers don't like stacking laser vias on top of each other because it can decrease the yield
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: A high-density module can be kept within standard PCB technology at 75 micron trace and space with 200 micron vias on an 81 to 85 micron drill; moving beyond that to substrate or interposer processes is a large step in price and closes the design to anyone without access to those processes.
claims.quote_verbatim: a trace width is 75 micron spacing as well. The vias are also quite small with 200 microns total diameter and 81 or 85 microns drill
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: A ten-layer any-layer board, small enough that 120 of them fit on an A4 sheet, cost about ten dollars each at that quantity, an order of magnitude below what the complexity of the process would suggest.
claims.quote_verbatim: having 120 of those PCBs each board costs us around $10
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: Turnaround time, not complexity, layer count, hole count or geography, is the dominant term in bare-board pricing: the same complex board is expensive tomorrow, moderate in a week, and very cheap if delivery date does not matter.
claims.quote_verbatim: for most, uh, circuit board manufacturing, the defining characteristic is actually like a turnaround time
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Paying for expedited fabrication buys queue position: the fab bumps other jobs and starts on the expedited board within minutes of the order. Eight to ten layer boards have been turned in 24 hours this way, at a cost of thousands of dollars for a prototype.
claims.quote_verbatim: it literally means they put you to the front of the queue, they bump everyone else's job
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Some fabs hold a line in reserve for emergency work and describe expedited jobs as bumping other customers when in fact they are spinning up that reserve capacity.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are companies that have like a dedicated line that they keep open for these emergency jobs
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Bare-board pricing is dominated by setup rather than per-unit cost at prototype quantities, so ordering twenty boards costs about the same as ordering one.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's about the same cost to order like 20 of them as it is to order just a single prototype
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: The same flatness of the cost curve extends further than most designers assume: quotes for ten and for 250 boards can differ little enough that the larger quantity is the rational order.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's not a big price difference between like 10 and 250
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Fabrication cost tracks the processing time of the panel rather than the material in it, which is why a small board on a shared panel is cheap and why board area matters less than the number of process passes.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's the cost of processing the panel
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Before online prototype services, a one-off commercial board cost of the order of a thousand dollars and took weeks, which is why home etching and point-to-point construction were rational choices rather than hobbies.
claims.quote_verbatim: you couldn't get one made commercially because it would cost you $1,000
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Mars, System Design & NAND - Mercurial Mars Mission

claims.claim_text: Inside companies in the early 1990s a board order meant eight hundred to a thousand dollars, a two-week wait and a triplicate purchase requisition, so an engineer who could etch a board in-house compressed a two-week loop into a day.
claims.quote_verbatim: it'd cost you 800 or a thousand bucks to get your board made. It'd take two weeks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Professionally made boards were out of reach for individuals until around the mid to late 1990s, costing thousands of dollars for a single board.
claims.quote_verbatim: They were thousands of dollars if you wanted to get one made
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: By the early 2010s a fixed-price online service supplied ten double-sided, plated-through, solder-masked and silkscreened boards for twelve dollars including tooling, a specification that had been the mark of a high-end kit a decade earlier.
claims.quote_verbatim: double-sided plate through solder mask, double-sided silkscreen board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bob Widlar, Electronic Design, FIRST Robotics - Monday, Meta Monday

claims.claim_text: Large four-layer boards of about 30 by 30 centimetres were quoted at roughly 175 dollars for five delivered, a size that had historically carried a large premium.
claims.quote_verbatim: 175 bucks for five boards of that size
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Four-layer prototype boards reached about seven dollars for five pieces at the low-cost Chinese shared-panel services, a change of roughly two orders of magnitude within a single career.
claims.quote_verbatim: I bought five boards for five, four layer boards with the seven bucks thing

claims.claim_text: Home fabrication schemes cannot change the economics while ten four-layer boards with solder mask and silkscreen cost about five dollars; the remaining case for making boards at home is turnaround measured in hours, not cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: None of these home PCB fabric, a do-it-yourself PCB fabrication things will ever be game-changing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Shared-panel prototype services at five dollars for five boards are not profitable in themselves; they are run as loss leaders or as a route to higher-value work.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't really run a profitable company doing a shared board service at those sort of prices
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Bare-board fabrication is a low-margin business, which is why assembly houses that consider bringing it in-house justify the move on turnaround time rather than on cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: Making PCBs is not a highly profitable proposition
claims.speaker: Chris Church
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: The cost and time of one hardware iteration fell from weeks and thousands of dollars to under a week and tens of dollars, which changes how many design spins a project can absorb.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'll get a board from JLCPCB in less than a week for 50 bucks
claims.speaker: Sergiy Nesterenko

claims.claim_text: A local fab willing to take artwork before late morning and ship the same day charged no more than about £150 for a double-sided Eurocard in 24 hours, a price that is defensible on a client project and not on a hobby one.
claims.quote_verbatim: one Eurocard done in 24 hours would be, it wouldn't be more than 150 quid all in
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Quick-turn prototype boards from a domestic fab still cost thousands of dollars, and engineers accustomed to low-cost overseas shared-panel pricing routinely mistake such a quote for an error.
claims.quote_verbatim: we were paying 2,000 bucks plus for a prototype board

claims.claim_text: The shared-panel prototype service began as a hobbyist group pooling designs onto one panel at a domestic fab, breaking the finished panel apart and distributing the boards, in response to month-long waits and poor yields from overseas orders.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had enough people in the group to justify our own panels from a U.S. fab
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: The measured defect rate through the domestic fabs used by that service was about one board in 40,000, against roughly one in four, and later about five percent, from the low-cost overseas orders it replaced. The defects were shorts, solder mask errors and annular ring breakouts.
claims.quote_verbatim: my failure rate through the US fabs is about one in 40,000 boards
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Overseas fabs can deliver the highest quality, but at a price that eliminates the cost advantage; normalised for turnaround and quality, top-tier domestic fabs are comparable, and matching a seven-day domestic delivery means paying for three-day service plus overnight shipping.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can get the utmost highest quality boards from China. You just pay for it
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: A shared-panel service can only pool designs that share a solder-mask colour, so the default colour runs daily and any other colour waits for enough orders to fill a panel.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you must have green, then that panel goes to the fab once a week instead of every day
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: A shared panel carries no room for special handling: with a hundred designs on the panel the fab will not adjust its process for one of them, whereas a customer paying for a full panel gets that attention.
claims.quote_verbatim: when they're mixing and matching, they don't want to dick around
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Fabrication pricing has pockets: a service that constrains the design to two or four layers, one solder-mask colour and a 0.1 millimetre track and gap can quote a much lower price and a three-day turnaround, and over half the orders on such a service fall inside that envelope.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you stick within the specs, it's like a 0.1 millimeter track gap, uh, then you're going to get a much more economic
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: A prototype house's low price comes from running every job through one fixed process. Supplying a fab drawing means specifying the process instead of accepting theirs, which is what makes non-standard work available and what makes it expensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: fab drawings mean that you're speccing everything out yourself

claims.claim_text: Combined rigid-flex construction cannot be ordered by uploading Gerbers alone; it requires the mechanical and stack-up definition that the standard prototype flow deliberately does not accept.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't just send your Gerbers off to the PCB manufacturer and forget about it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Fabs work in large standard panels, commonly quoted in inches at sizes such as 18 by 24, which frequently exceed the rail capacity of a pick-and-place machine. A panel intended for assembly must be sized for the assembly equipment, not for the fab's efficiency.
claims.quote_verbatim: Panels are large. The panels that they order from the manufacturers, they are large and often they will not fit in pick and place machines
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A six thou trace and space design is within reach of essentially every fab, so choosing that rule set keeps a design orderable from the cheapest shops and reproducible by anyone.
claims.quote_verbatim: The board uses a six mil, six mil process
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: A factory's habitual board house sets the design rules available to a project: a keyboard manufacturer's fab wanted 12 thou rules where the design needed 8, because keyboards are historically two-layer boards with wide traces and their supply chain is not set up for USB Type-C or fine-pitch parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: their usual PCB fab, they'd prefer that we were at 1212 rather than 8-8
claims.speaker: Jesse Vincent

claims.claim_text: BGA ball pitch propagates directly into fabrication cost, because finer pitch tightens the tolerances required on etching and solder mask. Moving a design from 0.4 to 0.8 millimetre pitch parts is what makes a board reproducible by its users.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have to use a 0.4 millimetre pin-pitch device, you're screwed
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard successors, CAD & Robots - Haussmannized Halloween Hypostrophe

claims.claim_text: Choosing the larger-pitch package variant of a processor is a deliberate fabrication decision on a physically large board, keeping the whole board inside the ordinary prototype-shop process instead of forcing high-density-interconnect construction across its full area.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're using the the larger pitch the 0.8 millimeter pitch BGA because we didn't want to do a high density board
claims.speaker: Werner Johansson
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: A 0.35 millimetre pitch wafer-level chip-scale package can be fabricated on a standard six-layer service with via-in-pad, but only by working exactly at the minimum 0.25 millimetre spacing and setting the design grid so every via lands on it; not all rows of the package can be escaped, and about 40 of 64 available pins were brought out.
claims.quote_verbatim: it is actually a 0.35 pitch bga
claims.episode_title: Like a steam engine in your house

claims.claim_text: Castellated edges and panel tabs compete for the same board perimeter: edges that are castellated cannot carry breakaway tabs, and a connector that overhangs the board edge removes another side, so panelisation must be planned together with the board outline.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's castellated edges, I couldn't have any tabs there either
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Designing below a fab's minimum track width does not necessarily produce a rejection; the boards arrive with shorts between adjacent traces, recoverable only by cutting them apart by hand.
claims.quote_verbatim: the track width was too small. Some of the tracks got short circuited

claims.claim_text: Design teams routinely define a layer order without dimensions and leave the dielectric thicknesses to the fabricator, effectively delegating the impedance calculation to whoever builds the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: won't specify any dimensions and just say to their fab guy, okay, you tell me the thickness of each of the layers
claims.speaker: Eric Bogatin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Bogatin - Tilded Thumb Tenets

claims.claim_text: Controlled impedance depends on a stack-up that belongs to one specific fab. Boards ordered from a different house without a fab drawing came back with impedance wrong by a factor of two, and two days were spent suspecting the measurement equipment before the stack-up was checked.
claims.quote_verbatim: the controlled impedance was off by 100%

claims.claim_text: Fabs work in metric while many designers work in thousandths of an inch, and a quoting page that presents both introduces a rounding error at the minimum-feature boundary, so a design that appears to pass the published rules is rejected or altered.
claims.quote_verbatim: they had a rounding error on their site
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Mixed unit conventions persist inside a single workflow, with track and space in thou and drills and board outlines in millimetres, because manufacturing is carried out in metric whatever units the designer used.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'll still use Imperial for track and space
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: The IPC standards define land patterns and pad dimensions for surface-mount components, and following them is what makes soldering reliable at manufacture; a footprint that is oversized or undersized relative to the standard degrades yield rather than merely looking wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: the IPC 7351. That's for surface mount components and manufacturing
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: A fabrication service can be operated without reading the IPC specifications, since they describe rather than police the process, but knowing them improves the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: I make a better product by knowing them
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Layout skill alone does not produce a manufacturable board. A designer who does not know the specific limitations of the fab, the assembler and the equipment the board will pass through produces designs that cannot be built, however sound the layout.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you don't know your limitations and capabilities of your system and your suppliers and your manufacturers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Guns and Mobile Labs - Nuanced Nomadic Non-essentials

claims.claim_text: Watching the process resolves design rules into physical causes: seeing a drill run explains why a via cannot shrink indefinitely, which no rule table conveys.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's why it's so important for people to visit factories and to learn about factory processes
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: A fabricator quoting against a supplied specification has no commercial interest in volunteering that a different stack-up or process would be cheaper; it will build what was asked for at the corresponding price. Learning which process the shop already runs is the designer's job.
claims.quote_verbatim: they wouldn't tell you like, here's the cheapest method

claims.claim_text: The same asymmetry appears across fabrication trades: a shop will accept a job that forces its most expensive process rather than suggest the small design change that would allow a cheaper one.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll just do it without telling you, Hey, if you just move these two things, we could do it for half the price
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Commercial fabs run an engineering review of incoming Gerbers before manufacture and query anything that looks wrong, which is a check the designer should expect and answer rather than a formality.
claims.quote_verbatim: A good PCB design house will, you know, question if they see something that's wrong
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Online design-for-manufacture tools that digitise the checks a board house performs, and return the result with a visualiser, remove the sales conversation from quoting; buyers select suppliers on that basis alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: They have a fantastic DFM tool. So you go upload your Gerbers on there

claims.claim_text: Manufacturers edit incoming board files to add panel rails and fiducials, and that edit can corrupt the design: on a four-layer board a via lost its layer assignment and was fabricated on the wrong layer, a fault that is neither a design error nor a process defect.
claims.quote_verbatim: Board files were being modified by the manufacturer to add rails and stuff like that. And a via lost data

claims.claim_text: Incoming inspection of bare boards exists to verify that the supplier built what was specified, and is a distinct activity from testing the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're checking the supplier sort of. So the PCB supplier
claims.episode_title: Motors on PCBs with Carl Bugeja

claims.claim_text: Board construction feeds back into assembly: taking a proven design to a much thicker board with heavier copper changed its thermal mass enough that every 0402 tombstoned in a reflow profile that had been dialled in for the thinner version.
claims.quote_verbatim: everything tombstone. All the 0402s, they all tombstone
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: The cost of an error is asymmetric between hardware and software because a fabricated and populated batch cannot be patched: ten thousand boards must be scrapped or reworked, and both are expensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: price of failure is much larger for hardware
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A symbol or footprint error that survives to fabrication costs the board run plus the days spent debugging a board that cannot work, which is why library errors are disproportionately expensive relative to their apparent triviality.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you, if you get something wrong in your symbol or footprint and you get that all the way through to fab
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: A defined checking procedure covering schematic, layout and footprints before release exists because the same defects cost far more once boards are in production than they do to catch on screen.
claims.quote_verbatim: How to check the schematic. How to check the layout, footprints and everything. Before it goes to production
claims.speaker: Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: A design that fails electromagnetic compliance typically consumes several board spins: a first failure, a speculative modification, another spin, pre-compliance retesting and a further formal test, reaching tens of thousands of dollars in board runs and test fees before salaries are counted.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can already count up the tens of thousands of dollars that they've spent just on the board runs and the testing
claims.speaker: Zachariah Peterson

claims.claim_text: Comparing fabricators' available stack-ups and prices at the start of a design, rather than at release, is what allows the manufacturing constraints to shape the layout while changes are still cheap.
claims.quote_verbatim: whatever you can do to pull that back as much as possible

claims.claim_text: Fabs will perform controlled-depth routing, embed components inside the board, and print multiple silkscreen colours, if the requirement is explained and paid for; these capabilities are outside the standard quoting flow rather than outside the industry.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can do controlled depth routing

claims.claim_text: Some fabricators can print resistors directly onto the board from conductive ink, supplying a specified resistance as part of the board rather than as a placed component.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've got a process to lay down, you know, you, if you need it, yeah, you need a 10K resistor
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: Solder mask, silkscreen and selective omission of layers give the board process a range of visual and mechanical effects, and boards can be stacked as structural layers to build an enclosure or front panel out of PCB material alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's many different techniques you can use with PCB manufacturing to get lots of different colors and textures
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PCB Mills, SDR and Oscilloscopes - Flaunting Furbelow Fanciness

claims.claim_text: Board dimensions outside the ordinary range, such as a board a metre long, restrict the design to the few fabs whose equipment can physically handle it.
claims.quote_verbatim: he had to find a specific board house that could do it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Flexible circuit material is not a recent technology; it was common in consumer equipment by the 1970s. What is new is rigid-flex construction with the flex layers laminated inside the stack-up rather than attached beneath it.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like a common in consumer gear, you know, even seventies consumer gear had, you know, flex PCB material
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Electronics fabrication capability is closer to binary than mechanical fabrication: a shop either can place an 0105 or cannot, and blind and buried vias have become common where they once were not, whereas mechanical suppliers vary continuously in equipment, engineering skill and quality control even when nominally able to make a part.
claims.quote_verbatim: most PCB fab houses that I use can do blind and buried videos
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Home etching carries a chemical disposal obligation that outsourced fabrication does not, which for many practitioners settles the question independently of cost or quality.
claims.quote_verbatim: why would I want to be trying to figure out if I can pour copper sulfide down the drain
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Magnets, China & IEEE - Xenomorphic Xerox Xebec

claims.claim_text: For laser-printed artwork, tracing paper of 90 gsm or heavier is the better transparency medium: lighter paper crinkles passing through the printer's fuser and drafting film distorts. Two sheets stapled into an envelope register the two sides of a double-sided board.
claims.quote_verbatim: thick tracing paper, 90 GSM or above, because the thinner stuff crinkles too much through the fuser
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Whether home fabrication is used at all turns on setup friction rather than capability: with tanks left standing and heating started at the beginning of a layout session, a simple breakout board is finished within the same session, whereas equipment stored away is never worth retrieving against a two or three day commercial turnaround.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a big difference between having tanks set up ready to go than having to, like, pull everything out of the cupboard
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Home fabrication reaches a double-sided board on proper FR4 with drilled holes in about an hour, but not plated-through holes, which is the capability boundary that sends all but the simplest work to a fab.
claims.quote_verbatim: it won't have plated through holes, but it'll have proper drilled holes
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shifting Away From DIY - Pedetentious PnP Progress

claims.claim_text: A milled prototype is not a fabrication-ready design: the layout must respect the mill's minimum feature and clearance, and a larger design is generally redrawn for the fab because the choices made for milling would not be made otherwise.
claims.quote_verbatim: he had to redo his board, even the layout around single chips
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: Prototypes are deliberately kept in the two-layer, standard-thickness envelope so that the prototype resembles the production board; thickness below the default 1.6 millimetres, at 0.6 or 0.8, is a routine order but layer count is where cost rises.
claims.quote_verbatim: I prefer to stay in the cheaper two-layer PCB territory because the cost goes up
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: Australia was reduced to a single bare-board manufacturer, which survived on government contracts, and its prototype pricing was of the order of a thousand dollars a board. Defence and in-country sourcing requirements, rather than commercial demand, are what keep such a fab alive.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was only one PCB manufacturer left in this entire country
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Domestic bare-board capacity can return by acquisition rather than by new investment; a New Zealand fab relocating to Australia restored a general-purpose bare-board option alongside the single remaining high-layer-count specialist.
claims.quote_verbatim: Circuit Labs in New Zealand is now in Australia

claims.claim_text: As designs grow more demanding, the set of board houses qualified to build them shrinks, and procurement rules requiring two or three competitive bids then route every job back to the same few suppliers, so the formal competition becomes nominal.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's fewer and fewer board houses that can do this sort of thing

claims.claim_text: Losing domestic prototype fabrication costs iteration speed, not just supply security. Much product innovation originates on the manufacturing side, so a team that hands the design over a wall gives up the feedback from watching it be built.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you lose the ability to prototype in your home country, you lose the ability to do rapid product iteration
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: The remaining Western fabrication and assembly shops are largely owned by proprietors approaching retirement, which has driven a wave of private-equity roll-ups in board fabrication and assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: they are owned by people that are kind of looking to retire
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: Vertical integration at scale has reappeared domestically: a satellite terminal producer runs bare-board fabrication, surface-mount assembly, functional test, injection moulding and box build on one site, shipping of the order of a thousand finished units a day.
claims.quote_verbatim: they manufacture the Starling terminals in the, in the US's biggest PCB assembly factory
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Choosing overseas manufacture by default ignores hidden costs; where a product's test procedure is technical and needs iteration to get right, a local facility at comparable pricing is the better choice, and pricing at good domestic shops can be close enough that proximity decides.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's huge hidden costs to going there
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe Grand - Pancyclopaedic Prototyping Polymath

claims.claim_text: For low volumes, working the total through — shipping, delay and quality risk included — can make local fabrication cheaper as well as less troublesome than an overseas order.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's cheaper by the time you work everything through
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin O'Flynn - Aspirated Adamantine Attacks

claims.claim_text: Contract assembly carries an arrangement lead time of five to ten days before anything is built, so a schedule of days rather than weeks forces in-house hand assembly regardless of volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: it takes five or 10 days just to arrange that
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: A hardware schedule is bounded by the fabrication step, which cannot begin until layout is finished and cannot be compressed below the fab's turnaround plus shipping; a board manufactured overnight overseas and flown in was the only way a ten-day build survived.
claims.quote_verbatim: get it manufactured overnight in Taiwan because we couldn't find a local manufacturer who would do it quick enough
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: Board fabrication and semiconductor fabrication respond very differently to urgency: a board can be expedited to hours because the queue is the constraint, while a chip with a 16 to 20 week process lead time cannot be, which is why distributors ask for months of forecast visibility rather than accepting expedite requests.
claims.quote_verbatim: a PCB can be turned around in like a day or, you know, hours
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Where one component forces an expensive process across a whole board, fabricating that component's escape on a small dense module and joining it to a cheap motherboard by castellations or a board-to-board connector costs less than paying the advanced process across the full board area.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's cheaper to get like a tiny little one inch by one inch board made, put the BGA on there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Where the manufacturer is known in advance, footprints and board features are designed for that fab and that assembly machine rather than to a generic standard, which forecloses moving the design elsewhere without rework.
claims.quote_verbatim: we would design the footprints and the boards specifically for that manufacturer and that assembly machine
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PCBs, Tektronix & Ham Radio - Habitual Handicraft Hangups

claims.claim_text: A stencil ordered alongside a board is cut from whichever revision was current when the order was placed, and the fab will not necessarily flag that later board revisions have moved parts; the mismatch appears at paste application.
claims.quote_verbatim: they made the stencil of the first design
claims.episode_title: Like a steam engine in your house
